statement: Gari Ledyard (Columbia University, PhD thesis 1966, revised 1998, additional paper 1997), following an earlier 1820 suggestion by Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat, proposed that 5-6 basic Hangul consonant shapes were adapted from the Mongol 'Phags-pa script (itself derived from Tibetan, created under Kublai Khan), transmitted via Korean exposure during the Yuan dynasty's suzerainty over Goryeo (1270-1356). This hypothesis is explicitly characterized in the literature as "less popular than the hypothesis that Hangul was largely an original invention" — a minority view. Even Ledyard's own account limits any Phagspa influence to a small subset of letter shapes and explicitly maintains that Hangul's innovative featural phonetic principle was an original Korean achievement.
scholarly_disagreement: Ledyard's 'Phags-pa-influence hypothesis (minority) vs. the mainstream original-invention position — both acknowledge the featural phonetic principle itself as an original Korean achievement regardless.

sources.citation: Ledyard, Gari K. PhD thesis (Columbia University, 1966, revised 1998) and 1997 paper on the 'Phags-pa/Hangul hypothesis.
sources.author: Gari Ledyard

interpretations.position: Hangul is largely an original invention, with the featural phonetic principle as a genuine Korean innovation

interpretations.strongest_case: The Hunminjeongeum Haerye itself, a contemporary primary document, credits Sejong and the Hall of Worthies scholars with the design.

interpretations.position: 5-6 basic consonant shapes were adapted from the Mongol 'Phags-pa script
interpretations.strongest_case: Documented Korean court exposure to 'Phags-pa via the Yuan dynasty's suzerainty over Goryeo (1270-1356), and specific shape correspondences Ledyard identifies for a handful of letters.
